title: Machine Learning Field Guide
audience: Readers with basic machine learning knowledge
scope: Original problem-first articles with worked examples, explanatory illustrations, and selected interactive demonstrations. Guided practices are omitted by request.

patterns.title: Hashed Feature
patterns.summary: Map a large or changing categorical vocabulary into a fixed feature space, accepting collisions in exchange for a bounded representation.
use_when: A categorical vocabulary is too large to maintain conveniently.
New category values arrive during serving.
The feature representation or model coefficient count must stay bounded.
example_user_queries: My categorical column has hundreds of thousands of values.
Our list of referring domains keeps growing.
New category values appear after we train the model.
One-hot encoding makes the model too large.
I cannot maintain a dictionary of every feature name.
How can I keep the input dimension fixed as new data arrives?
Two different categories seem to share a model weight.
How many positions should I allocate for categorical features?
Our training and serving code assign categories differently.
Will encoding an unfamiliar category teach the model what it means?
patterns.book_reference: Lakshmanan, Robinson, and Munn. Machine Learning Design Patterns. O'Reilly, 2020. Chapter 2: Hashed Feature.
patterns.difficulty: Basic ML knowledge; optional advanced notes on signed hashing

visual.reason: Expose collisions in a fixed-width representation and show what changes when the number of buckets increases.

example.normalization: Trim names; normalize Unicode NFC; preserve case; prefix channel=; ignore blank and repeated names

patterns.title: Active Learning
patterns.summary: Spend a limited labeling budget on examples selected to improve the current model, then refit and evaluate against an independent reference.
use_when: Expert annotations are expensive and unlabeled examples are plentiful.
Repeated labeling and retraining rounds are operationally feasible.
A query policy can be compared fairly against representative random labeling.
example_user_queries: We have thousands of examples but can only label a few hundred.

Can we improve this classifier without labeling the whole dataset?
Our reviewers keep labeling near-identical easy cases.
The model is uncertain about lots of examples; where do we start?
Should we choose difficult examples or label a random sample?
How do I measure whether selective labeling is actually helping?
Our label budget is spent but some groups are still poorly modeled.
Can choosing new training data make the model worse?
When should we stop asking people for more annotations?
patterns.difficulty: Basic ML knowledge; transparent small-model learning sandbox

visual.reason: Compare identical starting models and equal label budgets, exposing both selected labels and refitted cutoff intervals.

limitations: One monotonic noiseless boundary
Equal label costs
Fixed independent synthetic evaluation set
No general annotation-savings claim

patterns.title: Weak Supervision
patterns.summary: Turn imperfect rules, existing records, and other noisy signals into training labels while tracking their coverage, conflicts, and shared errors.
use_when: Unlabeled examples are plentiful but verified training labels are scarce.
Domain knowledge can be expressed as reusable rules, lookups, or noisy labeling sources.
Multiple imperfect sources can be evaluated and combined under explicit assumptions.
example_user_queries: We have lots of unlabeled documents and a few useful rules.
Can existing business rules help us build training data?
Our labeling sources disagree about the same records.
How do I combine noisy labels without pretending they are correct?
We cannot afford to annotate every example by hand.
Several of our labeling rules seem to repeat the same clue.
What should happen when none of our rules matches?
Can a database provide labels for our text classifier?
Our automatically generated training labels are biased.
How do I know whether better label coverage improves the final model?
Can we train a model that generalizes beyond our keyword rules?
How should we evaluate a classifier trained on imperfect labels?

visual.reason: Make abstention, conflicting votes, and the effect of copying a source visible without implying calibrated probabilities.

limitations: Assigned weights are not estimated source accuracies

patterns.title: Label-Preserving Augmentation
patterns.summary: Create additional training views by changing aspects of an example that should not change its target, while checking that the relevant evidence survives.
use_when: Labeled originals are limited and realistic nuisance variation is understood.
A transformation policy can be checked against the task definition and deployment conditions.
Training should discourage dependence on irrelevant viewpoint, exposure, or acquisition differences.
example_user_queries: Our image model works in the studio but fails on customer photographs.
Can I get more training variation without labeling every new image?
Which image transformations are safe for this target?
Flipping an image seems to change the answer we want.
How do I keep bounding boxes aligned when augmenting images?
Our augmented text examples sometimes reverse the sentiment.
How strong should our crops or color changes be?
We generated many extra images but they look almost identical.
Could augmented copies be leaking into the test set?
How can I tell if augmentation helps a rare class?
Is changing an input while keeping its label always valid?
Should training-time image changes also run during evaluation?
patterns.difficulty: Basic ML knowledge; exact synthetic transformation explorer

visual.reason: Show that one actual pixel transformation preserves arrow presence while changing arrow direction.

limitations: Exact finite synthetic templates; no learned semantic judgment

No camera noise, perceptual threshold, classifier training, or accuracy estimate

patterns.title: Self-Supervised Pretraining
patterns.summary: Learn reusable model parameters from prediction tasks constructed from raw data, then adapt and evaluate them on the task that matters.
use_when: Raw data is plentiful but downstream task labels are scarce.
A self-created prediction task can plausibly teach transferable structure.
An appropriate pretrained checkpoint can be adapted and independently evaluated.
goals: Separate representation learning from task adaptation
mechanisms: Reuse and adaptation of learned parameters
example_user_queries: We have millions of messages but only a few hundred intent labels.
Can our unlabeled data help before we train the classifier?
How does predicting missing words help a different task?
Should we train a model from scratch or adapt an existing checkpoint?
Our pretraining loss improved but the classifier did not.
What is the difference between masked prediction and next-token prediction?
Can we learn image features without category annotations?
How should we test whether pretrained representations are useful?
When should we freeze the encoder instead of fine-tuning it?
Could our pretraining corpus contaminate evaluation?
Does a larger raw corpus always produce a better starting model?
Where do the training targets come from if the data has no labels?
patterns.difficulty: Basic ML knowledge; miniature conditional word-count model

visual.reason: Separate automatically constructed pretext targets from independently supplied downstream labels, with a computed token-probability explorer.

example.masked_context: Immediate left and right words, with [BOS] / [EOS] boundaries
limitations: Conditional count tables, not neural embeddings
Five fixed fictional lines; no measured transfer or downstream accuracy
Both queries excluded from training; fixed vocabulary
Masked predictor uses only immediate neighbors; causal predictor only the preceding word

patterns.title: Knowledge Distillation
patterns.summary: Train a student to reproduce useful behavior from a teacher, often combining teacher probabilities with verified labels to meet deployment constraints.
use_when: A useful teacher or ensemble is too expensive for the intended deployment.
Representative transfer inputs and informative teacher outputs are available.
A student can be compared fairly against training without distillation and measured on target hardware.
goals: Preserve task quality in a student model
example_user_queries: Our ensemble is accurate but too slow to serve.
Can we train a small model to imitate our large model?
What do teacher probabilities offer beyond a winning class label?
How should we combine teacher outputs with verified labels?
What does temperature change during distillation?
Our student matches the teacher but makes more label errors.
How can I compare distillation with training the same student normally?
We need a model that fits within a phone memory and latency budget.
Can our teacher and student have different architectures?
Does a lower imitation loss mean better task performance?
Can we distill a service that returns only generated text?
How do we know the smaller model will actually run faster?
patterns.difficulty: Basic ML knowledge; optional explicit distillation objective and gradient

visual.reason: Show softened teacher probabilities, separate hard-label supervision, actual student updates, and temperature-one deployment.

example.alpha_definition: Weight on teacher matching; hard-label weight is 1 - alpha
limitations: One example with three free scores, not a neural student

Fixed three-class teacher and true Delivery label

patterns.title: Decision-Focused Learning
patterns.summary: Train predictions for the quality of the constrained decisions they induce, while keeping the objective, feasible actions, and evaluation assumptions explicit.
use_when: Predictions feed an explicit optimization problem with meaningful operational costs or benefits.
Prediction errors have different consequences depending on constraints and competing actions.
Decision outcomes can be evaluated using complete labels or a justified outcome model.
goals: Evaluate prediction and decision metrics separately
example_user_queries: Our forecasts improved but our schedules got worse.
How can we train predictions for the decisions they drive?
The model with lower MSE does not choose the most valuable jobs.
Our predictions feed a capacity-constrained allocation solver.
Which prediction mistakes actually change the chosen action?
How should we compare two models used inside an optimizer?
What does regret measure in a predict-then-optimize system?
We need to account for unequal shortages and excess inventory.
Can we learn through a solver that makes discrete decisions?
Our capacity limits changed; do our model scores still make sense?
We only observed outcomes for past selected actions.
Does zero training regret mean our future decisions will be reliable?
patterns.difficulty: Basic ML knowledge; exact finite-grid fitting and subset optimization

visual.reason: Fit the same predictor family to prediction error or decision regret and expose exact resulting allocations and outcomes.

example.solver: Exact maximization over all feasible subsets of three indivisible jobs
example.solver_ties: Fewer jobs, then alphabetical subset order; objective tolerance 1e-9
limitations: One fully observed training instance, not held-out generalization
Known capacity costs and additive nonnegative benefits
Exhaustive finite-grid fitting, not a differentiable solver or SPO+
Task-specific predictions need not be calibrated benefit forecasts

patterns.title: Leakage-Safe Evaluation
patterns.summary: Design evaluation around the intended prediction setting, preventing unavailable information and related examples from crossing the relevant learning boundaries.
use_when: Offline model scores support selection or deployment decisions.
Records share customers, devices, source documents, duplicates, or overlapping windows.
Features or labels arrive after their event timestamps, or preprocessing learns from data.
goals: Make performance claims match deployment conditions
Keep evaluation information outside fitting and selection
Identify the independent units being evaluated
example_user_queries: Our test score is excellent but performance collapses for new customers.
Can visits from the same patient appear in training and test?
How should we split data when predictions are made in the future?
A complaint happened yesterday but reached our system today; can we use it?
Should we normalize features before splitting the dataset?
Does a pipeline prevent every kind of data leakage?
How do we handle labels that become available weeks later?
When is random row splitting appropriate?
Why does group holdout produce a much lower score?
Can we tune thresholds on the final test set?
Does stratification keep related images out of both sets?
How do we avoid a target encoder learning a row’s own label?
patterns.difficulty: Basic ML knowledge; dataset boundaries, majority predictors, and prediction-time availability

visual.reason: Fit the same ID learner under equal-sized visit and customer holdouts, exposing actual identity overlap and computed scores.

limitations: Stable within-customer labels and no transferable features
Grouped test rows represent four distinct customers
Identity separation does not establish time safety
Prediction question changes interpretation, not scores
Visit holdout assumes first-visit labels were available

patterns.title: Behavioral Testing
patterns.summary: Turn important expectations about model behavior into executable examples and input-output relations, revealing failures that aggregate scores can hide.
use_when: Aggregate model quality hides important task-specific failures.
A model replacement must preserve known capabilities and avoid regressions.
Expected labels or justified relationships between predictions can be stated explicitly.
example_user_queries: Our model has good accuracy but fails on obvious examples.
How can we check whether a classifier understands simple negation?
Adding an irrelevant name changes the sentiment score.
We need to compare a replacement model with the current service.
Can we test a model without knowing its internal architecture?
How do we turn a production failure into a regression check?
Our consistency checks pass even for a constant model.
When should a change to an input preserve its prediction?
How do we choose tolerances for paired model tests?
We generated thousands of examples but they all test the same behavior.
Our test suite improved after we loosened its assertions.
Can a model pass directional tests while giving wrong labels?
patterns.difficulty: Basic ML knowledge; explicit labels, scalar scores, and paired comparisons

visual.reason: Compare the same computed outputs against distinct behavioral expectations and expose constant-predictor and tolerance loopholes.

limitations: Handwritten rules, no trained or external model
Constructed scores are not calibrated probabilities
Immediate preceding-token negation only
Fixed synthetic suite, not deployment prevalence or demographic fairness
Non-increasing permits unchanged outputs
Constant predictor can pass all relational tests

patterns.title: Slice-Based Evaluation
patterns.summary: Evaluate the same predictions on meaningful subsets, retaining sample sizes and uncertainty so aggregate improvements do not conceal local failures.
use_when: A model serves varied user populations or operating conditions.
An aggregate improvement may conceal local regressions during model replacement.
Incidents or underrepresented intersections need focused investigation.
goals: Compare models on the same examples
Retain denominators and uncertainty for small or empty groups
example_user_queries: Our average accuracy improved but desktop users are doing worse.
Which groups or conditions does our model fail on?
How can we compare two models without hiding local regressions?
The worst group has only one labeled example.
How should we report an empty evaluation group?
Our language and device groups overlap; can we add their counts?
Can we average subgroup scores to get overall accuracy?
Recall and accuracy tell different stories for this group.
What happens when deployment has a different device mix?
We searched hundreds of subgroups and found a bad one.
Does hiding small groups make our evaluation more reliable?
Do equal group accuracies establish that a model is fair?
patterns.difficulty: Basic ML knowledge; fractions, confusion matrices, and uncertainty interpretation

visual.reason: Compute identical overall predictions by device, language, intersections, and overlapping conditions while exposing support and undefined metrics.

limitations: Fixed fictional records and predicted labels, no model training
Independent binomial assumption for illustrative separate-model intervals
Not paired-difference or simultaneous search-adjusted intervals
Overlapping memberships are not independent evidence
Display support filters do not resolve hidden groups
No causal, population, or demographic fairness conclusion

patterns.title: Probability Calibration
patterns.summary: Fit and validate a mapping from model scores to probabilities whose stated likelihoods agree with observed event frequencies in the intended setting.
use_when: Predicted probabilities inform expected costs, planning, risk communication, or confidence-based routing.
Good rankings or class accuracy coexist with probability estimates that are too extreme or too cautious.
Independent labeled evidence can support calibration and subsequent evaluation.
goals: Separate probability quality from class accuracy
mechanisms: Positive temperature fitted by log loss
Reliability diagrams and proper scoring rules
example_user_queries: When our model says 80 percent, the event happens far less often.
Our model ranks cases well but its probabilities seem too extreme.
Can probability estimates improve without changing accuracy?
How can we fit a calibration mapping without using test labels?
Does a lower Brier loss prove that probabilities are calibrated?
Our reliability diagram looks perfect after pooling every score.
We need probabilities for a cost-based decision threshold.
Can one temperature fix biased probabilities for every group?
The probabilities changed after we updated the base model.
Our calibration worked offline but failed on another population.
What is the difference between softened teacher outputs and calibration?
Are prediction-set coverage and class probabilities the same guarantee?
patterns.difficulty: Basic ML knowledge; binary probabilities, logits, and independent evaluation

visual.reason: Fit a bounded temperature using calibration records only, compare independent probability losses, and expose binning cancellation without changing classes.

assumptions: Certain prevention of the modeled loss if issue exists

limitations: Frozen synthetic base logits and twenty cases per split

Evaluation labels and bin counts never fit temperature

No population, subgroup, or distribution-shift guarantee

patterns.title: Conformal Prediction
patterns.summary: Use held-out prediction errors to construct sets or intervals with finite-sample marginal coverage under exchangeability, while measuring how informative those sets remain.
use_when: A system can use prediction intervals or possible-label sets instead of only point outputs.
A stated marginal coverage target matters and exchangeable calibration evidence is plausible.
Set size, interval width, and subgroup coverage can be evaluated alongside the target.
goals: Construct outcome sets with explicit coverage assumptions
Keep finite-sample correction and edge cases visible
Evaluate set usefulness and uneven coverage
mechanisms: Candidate inclusion below the score threshold
example_user_queries: Our model gives a point estimate but we need a planning interval.
What does a ninety-percent prediction interval actually promise?
Can we make uncertainty sets without assuming Gaussian errors?

Our overall coverage is good but difficult cases are often missed.
Do conformal intervals have to be the same width everywhere?
How should we keep calibration and evaluation data separate?
Can a classifier return several plausible labels?

Can we narrow a prediction interval just to make it useful?
Does shuffling time-series data make the coverage guarantee valid?
How do coverage guarantees differ from calibrated class probabilities?
patterns.difficulty: Basic ML knowledge; residuals, sorted ranks, and marginal coverage

visual.reason: Calculate residual ranks and intervals, preserve the unbounded quantile edge case, and compare overall and subgroup evaluation coverage.

limitations: Fixed synthetic model predictions and labels
Marginal coverage assumes exchangeable calibration and new observations
Not conditional on each calibration sample, input, or subgroup
Finite evaluation batches need not achieve the target percentage
Unbounded interval when corrected rank exceeds calibration count
No trained model, external service, or verified operational exchangeability

patterns.title: Selective Prediction
patterns.summary: Give a predictor an explicit abstention route, and evaluate accepted errors, automation coverage, and the cost of handling deferred cases together.
use_when: Incorrect automatic decisions are costly and a viable review or fallback route exists.
Automation must grow within a measurable accepted-error and workload budget.
Confident mistakes and subgroup differences need examination before choosing a gate.
goals: Reduce harmful automatic errors while tracking how much work is automated
Make abstention consequences and capacity explicit
Separate observed selective risk from statistical guarantees
mechanisms: Explicit fallback capacity and cost accounting

visual.reason: Show which fixed predictions are released, calculate risk and coverage, and expose subgroup disparities, nonmonotone observed risk, and review capacity.

patterns.title: Schema-Based Data Validation
patterns.summary: Express the expected structure and constraints of model inputs as a versioned contract, check incoming data against it, and make violations actionable before they propagate.
use_when: Changing exports and multiple producers feed model training or prediction interfaces.
Silent coercion or permissive storage hides broken input assumptions.
Training and serving require compatible shared features with explicit label differences.
goals: Make validation findings and release policy distinct
Keep semantic blind spots and schema evolution visible
mechanisms: Versioned field requirements and scalar types
Inclusive numeric bounds and category domains
Recorded explicit conversions and whole-batch hold
example_user_queries: Our training job runs even when an upstream export changes types.
A feature that used to be numeric is arriving as text.
How can we catch missing labels before retraining?

Should we convert numeric strings or reject them?

patterns.difficulty: Basic ML knowledge; data types, required fields, and model input boundaries

visual.reason: Execute explicit field checks, separate row and violation counts, compare training and serving contracts, and show a semantic unit mismatch that passes numeric rules.

example.disposition: Any violation holds the whole batch; passing rows are not released independently.
example.scope: Original teaching validator, not a complete schema library; unit metadata is absent and semantic units are not validated.

patterns.title: Point-in-Time Feature Retrieval
patterns.summary: Reconstruct features for each historical decision using the right entity, time cutoff, availability history, and freshness policy, while retaining decisions with missing matches.
use_when: Historical decisions are joined to changing feature values for training or backtesting.
Sources arrive late or historical snapshots receive later corrections.
Feature freshness and missing matches must agree with the intended prediction path.
goals: Prevent historical examples from seeing unavailable versions
Make entity, event, availability, and age constraints explicit
Preserve decisions with missing feature matches
mechanisms: Ranking eligible snapshots before version selection
Explicit age limits and null-preserving results
example_user_queries: Our offline model seems to use information from after the prediction.
How should we join changing features to historical labels?

Do event-time joins exclude corrections written later?

patterns.difficulty: Basic ML knowledge; entity keys, timestamp comparisons, and feature snapshots

visual.reason: Compute two-clock candidate eligibility, compare three retrieval policies, and expose late arrivals, later corrections, age boundaries, and null-preserving missing matches.

example.scope: Scalar snapshots, not raw event aggregates. Availability is assumed to mean actual prediction-path availability; execution logs and model accuracy are not simulated.

patterns.title: Shadow Deployment
patterns.summary: Run a candidate alongside the live model on copied requests, keep its outputs off the user response path, and evaluate operational behavior and matched predictions before changing serving authority.
use_when: A model or serving-stack change has passed offline checks but needs live-input operational evidence.
Latency, dependency compatibility, or capacity is uncertain before changing user-facing predictions.
Matched candidate/incumbent comparisons can be logged without production side effects.
goals: Exercise a candidate while the incumbent retains serving authority
Separate operational success from labeled prediction quality
Expose response and label missingness before promotion
mechanisms: Isolated candidate capacity and disabled side effects
Separate mirroring, response, and labeled-pair denominators
example_user_queries: Our new model passed offline tests but we need to see live inputs first.
Can we run a replacement model without showing its predictions to users?
How do we compare a candidate with the incumbent on the same requests?

How much extra inference work does mirroring create?

patterns.summary: Release a model to a limited share of real traffic, expand only when predefined evidence permits, and restore the incumbent when guardrails fail.

Traffic can be partitioned and the incumbent can take back the load.

Limited randomization among eligible actions has an acceptable operating cost.
goals: Collect informative feedback beyond the current policy

How can we learn from clicks without treating unseen items as failures?

patterns.summary: Train a shared model through coordinated local learning at separate data holders, aggregating compatible updates while accounting for participation, unequal data, and explicit privacy mechanisms.
use_when: Useful training records remain with separately controlled devices or organizations.
Participants share a task and can agree on model, feature, and training conventions.
Pooling raw records is undesirable or impractical, and orchestration costs are justified.
goals: Make participation and weighting objectives explicit

Compose privacy costs across training accesses

goals: Improve the worst measured group loss
